text: wsl-claude: yes, exactly. Both hash and timestamp are non-unique but valuable: each is an INDEX, a fast way in by the question you're asking. Hash answers 'what happened to this message'; timestamp answers 'what happened since then'. Neither identifies a row; seq does. One unique key, several non-unique indexes: the ordinary shape for a log.
so to enter a new row, sequence would be read from the end to find the last used sequence number?
so to enter a new row, sequence would be read from the end to find the last used sequence number?

No, nobody reads it. With AUTOINCREMENT, SQLite keeps the last number used in a tiny table of its own (sqlite_sequence, one row per table), and the insert takes the next one itself. The node just says 'insert this row' and gets the new seq back. It costs the same whether the log has 10 rows or 10 million, and because that counter only ever goes up, a number is never handed out twice, even after the newest rows are deleted.

wsl-claude: no, the database hands it out. The insert simply leaves seq out, and SQLite assigns the next number itself. With AUTOINCREMENT it keeps the highest number ever used in one tiny bookkeeping row (the sqlite_sequence table), so nothing is read from the end, and two writes can never get the same number: only one write happens at a time. The writer learns which number it got straight from the insert (lastInsertRowid). Checked just now on node's own SQLite: rows got 1 and 2; after deleting row 2, the next insert got 3, not 2 again.

sequence will be the key returned by searches?
sequence will be the key returned by searches?

Inside the log, yes: every search finds rows by seq. Outside, not yet, because of this plan's rule 1: nothing above trafficLog.js changes, so searches return rows exactly as today, without seq. Returning it would be a small addition, one more field on each row, and a useful one. It fits your 'every list is a search, bucket-bounded, with a partial flag': a partial answer would say 'continue after seq N', which can't skip or repeat a row the way 'since this time' can. But it's a change to the interface, so it's yours: either rule 1 allows that one addition, or it waits for a later plan.

wsl-claude: agree with claude-windows, and it's less new than it sounds. The owner's record ALREADY pages 'by position', a row's place in the file (server.js:1798, 'read a page at a time... why it pages by position', via trafficLog.history). seq IS that position, made permanent: today 'position 5000' only holds while nothing before it moves; in the table, seq 5000 means that row forever. So returning seq is just naming the cursor the record already uses. And when the searches (the G2 pattern) come to the log, seq is the natural key: search -> (seq, label) pairs, get(seq) -> the row.
